endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Structured public feedback can be used to evaluate whether GAI systems are performing as intended and to calibrate and verify traditional measurement methods.

endorsements.title: Strengthening ethics review of the development of artificial intelligence (AI) systems in health research: a guide for research ethics committees in Uganda
endorsements.quote: The strategies should be reviewed by the REC to ensure that they respect participants and research communities’ values, interests and dignity.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether applying human-subjects protections or IRB review to AI feedback and engagement participants prevents unethical treatment, and no study documents the hazard itself. Support rests on two endorsements, a federal framework that frames structured feedback as permissive and a research ethics guide from Uganda that recommends committee review.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The two endorsements are a framework and a commentary, and neither reports outcome data on participant harm or protection.

NIST AI 600-1 uses permissive language and describes structured public feedback as a way to evaluate generative AI systems, without addressing participant protections directly. The Uganda research ethics guide states that engagement strategies should be reviewed by a research ethics committee to protect participants' values, interests, and dignity. The two sources differ in strength and jurisdiction.

With no studies supplied, no data describe how feedback participants from Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups are treated, or whether review processes change their experience. The Uganda guide refers to research communities' values, but it offers guidance rather than measured results.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI feedback and engagement activities conducted with and without human-subjects review, measuring consent quality, participant understanding, complaints, reported harms, and withdrawal rates. Descriptive work documenting how often these activities currently receive IRB or ethics committee review would also establish whether the hazard occurs in practice.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy participants. Health systems that recruit these groups for AI feedback activities cannot draw on data showing whether review protects them, and any protections adopted would rest on ethical principle and endorsement rather than measured effect.
